title: Well spoken
hook: speech that is well spoken, pleasant, true and in line with the teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mara's generals, the army with names like craving, sloth, fear and doubt, and your line, better to fight than yield. Which general showed up for you? Today closes a week, and it's about the mouth. Day six hundred two.

Count the words you'll say today. Researchers have tried, and the estimates run into the thousands. Most of them vanish the moment they're spoken: please pass the salt, running late, sounds good. A few stay. A sentence someone said to you at twelve years old can still be sitting in you at forty, for good or for ill. The early Buddhist texts take speech very seriously, because it's the one act most of us do all day long without thinking. In the third chapter of the Sutta Nipata there's a short discourse that sets out what makes speech good. It has four marks, and a poet stands up at the end. Today: well spoken.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF WORDS A DAY.` → `A FEW STAY FOR YEARS.` → `SUTTA NIPATA 3.3.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells the monks that speech with four marks is well spoken, blameless and not faulted by the wise. The monk says only what is well spoken, not what is badly spoken. Only what is in line with the teaching, not what goes against it. Only what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant. Only what is true, not what is false. Four filters, and every sentence has to pass all four. Then something lovely happens. Vangisa, the poet monk you met three days ago asking after his teacher, stands up and says: something has come to me. And he puts the teaching into verse on the spot. Speak only words, he says, that don't torment yourself and don't harm others. Speak pleasant words, words people are glad to hear, without bringing in anything bad. Truth, he says, is the deathless word; on truth the good stand firm. Notice what this is not. It isn't flattery: pleasant is joined to true. And it isn't blunt honesty with no care for the listener: true is joined to pleasant. The two hold each other in check. Look back at the week. A mind unshaken. The old way of the brahmins. The boatman who takes others across. Vangisa's question about his teacher. The young wanderer's promise to a king, kept. And Mara's generals. Today the poet comes back, and he's still doing what he does best: finding the right words.
screen: `FOUR MARKS OF GOOD SPEECH.` · `WELL SAID, THE TEACHING, PLEASANT, TRUE.` · `VANGISA PUTS IT IN VERSE.` · `TRUTH IS THE DEATHLESS WORD.` · then, large: `WELL SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak well once. Sit and settle. Bring to mind one conversation you'll have today, at work, at home, on the phone. Pick one thing you'll need to say in it. Now run it through Vangisa's test, gently. Is it true? Will it harm the person hearing it, or you? Can it be said in a way they'd be glad to hear, without bending the truth? Find the words, then let them go and rest with the breath. When the moment comes, you'll have them ready. The bell holds the time.
Well spoken. In the Sutta Nipata, speech that is well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true, all four at once. Today's word.
Your line: well spoken. Today, say one thing that is both true and kind, on purpose, to someone who will be glad to hear it. Day six hundred two.

howItsDone: Right speech is the third factor of the noble eightfold path, and many Buddhists, lay and ordained, keep a precept against false speech; teachers often give the four marks of well-spoken words as a test before speaking.

pairs: the poet monk who put it in verse
joined to true, so not flattery
joined to pleasant, so not cruelty

myth: in Sn 3.3, speech only has to be true to count as well spoken
it has four marks: well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true.
the poet Vangisa turns the teaching into verse right there
he stands up, says something has come to him, and praises it in verse.
Vangisa calls truth the deathless word
in his verses, truth is the deathless word, and the good stand firm on it.

fork.setup: you're Vangisa. the Buddha has just finished teaching four marks of good speech, and a verse is rising in you. what do you do?
options: keep quiet; it isn't your place.
stand, say something has come to you, and speak it in verse.
write it down later for yourself.
fork.reveal: he stands, tells the Buddha a verse has come to him, and is invited to speak it. the teaching gets its poem on the spot.

original.note: Pali subhasita: well spoken. the Subhasita Sutta is Sn 3.3.

trapdoor: what you thought: good speech just means not lying.
what it means: four marks at once: well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true, each keeping the others in check.
what a scholar hears: the Subhasita Sutta (Sn 3.3) is also found in the Samyutta Nikaya, in the section of verses connected with Vangisa (SN 8.5).

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 3.3 (Subhasita Sutta), the four marks and Vangisa's verses

notes: Sn 3.3 paraphrased. Fausbøll's 1881 translation (SBE 10) is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.
Confirm the order of the four marks and that Vangisa's verses include 'truth is the deathless word' (sacca ve amata vaca).
